summary: Source-anchored research for Source-domain collapse in LLM metaphor. Run status: COMPLETED.

facts.text: Artificial Hivemind (NeurIPS 2025 Datasets & Benchmarks oral) documents mode collapse in open-ended generation on 26K real-world queries: intra-model repetition and, more strongly, inter-model homogeneity, where different models produce strikingly similar outputs. This is the general mechanism that would make the same vehicle domains recur across vendors. (medium confidence)

Even when told to avoid metaphor, 6.27% of ChatGPT's text stayed metaphorical, and its metaphor identification differed significantly from a human linguist's: metaphor is used rhetorically without tracking conceptual boundaries, which is the condition under which mixed or ill-fitting source domains slip through. (low confidence)
The same study found source-domain variety rose for abstract targets (Politics used 21 distinct source domains), so collapse is topic-dependent rather than uniform. (low confidence)

A 2026 computational audit (Chang, Qu, Li, arXiv 2604.04732) reports 'representational collapse': LLMs flatten culturally distinct metaphorical framings, with some prompts (e.g. metaphors for Death under India and China personas) yielding compact clusters that reuse essentially one metaphor; a cultural persona sometimes narrows rather than widens the metaphor space. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-09-23)

LLM-generated metaphor norms track word-co-occurrence properties (familiarity, metaphoricity) well but track aptness and concreteness, which need topic-vehicle reasoning, only weakly to moderately. That fits vehicle choice driven by frequency rather than fit. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-09-23)

In a 20-speech ChatGPT corpus (10 topics, MIPVU-coded), the model heavily favoured the Planting source domain across Education, Economy and Health (e.g. 'sowing seeds of growth', 'cultivating knowledge'): one vehicle domain reused across unrelated targets. (low confidence)
